MABUZA PROTECTION ORDER

By: Anna-Maria van Niekerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Has one man's long lonely battle to build his dream Big-5 reserve inadvertently opened a way for ordinary people to hit back decisively against corruption?

Unique Selling Point:
After 20 years of struggling through the courts, spending R18-million in legal fees to defend his actions to establish a luxury Big-5 game Nkomazi Game reserve, Cradle of Life, Mpumalanga businessman Fred Daniel has finally broken through against ongoing harassment and high-level corruption that have nearly scuppered his life’s work – by applying a simple, inexpensive and bold law.

Conservationist Fred Daniel made his fortune in IT and dreamed of establishing a big-5 game reserve near Badplaas, Mpumalanga. He had all the partnerships and international deals in place to make it happen. Daniel bought up 98 failing farms near Badplaas – it had become impossible to cultivate grain here, and farmers were eager to sell up and get out.

But since Day One, Daniel has found himself at the receiving end of administrative blockages, violence, victimisation and harassment, last year there was an attempted media smear campaign with false allegations that Daniel had to refute by opening his gates and books to the media.

And he's even had a phone call from one David Mabuza, then MEC for Agriculture, to get out of Badplaas.

He couldn’t get his Big-5 permits. He had his boundary fences cut. There were attempts to burn down his buildings. He woke up to violent protests on his doorstep. He had his animals removed and sold off with the money diverted to the Problem Animal Fund.

And then there was the fraudulent land claim against his land -- the scandal that saw the department of rural development and land reform buying farms for claimant communities at rates that were up to 300% higher than market value.

Daniel hired forensic investigators and exposed the fraudulent land claim (in 2003), with tentacles reaching into the then MEC for Agriculture, DD Mabuza’s office. If Daniel hadn't exposed it, the tax payer would have lost R600million. Since then Parliament have even passed the Restitution of Land Rights Amendment Act, 2014 which provides that anyone who lodges a claim with the intention of defrauding the state shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine and imprisonment. (Two years ago the Land Claims Court in Randburg ordered Rural Development and Land Reform Minister Gugile Nkwinti to take back the land that was given to a controversial trust and review the claim. The validity of the claim involving 105 farms worth R51 million in Mpumalanga’s Badplaas area had been contested over the past 12 years.)

But none such provisions protected Daniel when he turned whistleblower.

Daniel's whistleblowing, together with defrauded land claimants, resulted the scheme exposed and a R3.3 million fraud charge being laid by the EFF against Mpumalanga Premier David Mabuza (http://city-press.news24.com/News/r33m-haunts-premier-mabuza-20151212).

But by then, Daniel's investors, and potential partners had vanished.

But all hell broke loose. Harassment escalated sharply.

Of 20 court cases where Daniel opposed the Mpumalanga tourism authorities’ administrative interference, he won 18. In the process he spent over R18-million.

In forensic reports and court proceedings, all of which Daniel paid for, testimony emanated that officials had suffered immense political pressure, all the way to the Premier's office, to thwart Cradle of Life.

Now, only two cases remain outstanding:

- a R1,6bn damages claim against the government for the business he’s lost (mediation process is underway to try and settle this and restore relationships with new Tourism Authority management who are eager to help him).

- an interim protection order against the same DD Mabuza – now Premier of Mpumalanga and Deputy President of the ANC.



Summary:
This is a story of Fred Daniel’s breakthrough after 20 years of legal struggles – through the clever, lateral application of the relatively simple Protection from Harassment Act (17 of 2011) which came into effect in 2013 to stop and fix harassment and stalking behaviour which violate someone’s Constitutional right to privacy and dignity.

After spending millions on legal representatives, investigations and getting nowhere, this Act provided for Daniel an inexpensive civil remedy to protect him from behaviour which may not constitute a crime but may impact negatively on various rights...

All he had to do was fill out a simple form, available online, and put his case to a Magistrate – which Daniel did in Carolina.

He didn’t even need legal representation. And his harasser didn't have to be present.

The only risk...if Daniel is lying, he could himself face arrest.

On Monday 29 January, the Carolina Magistrate granted Daniel his interim protection order, and the court has invited Mr Mabuza to court on 19 Feb to explain why the order shouldn’t be made permanent.





Further information:
MEDIATION FINALLY PAID!

Daniel has been going out of his way to stay out of the courts -- and his efforts finally paid off when he found Stellenbosch attorney Jacques Joubert last year, who specialises in mediation and has been knocking on every door in Mpumalanga to STOP running to court and opposing every action, and sitting down to mediate a way forward.

Joubert convinced the new Tourism Management last year that mediation is a private, confidential and without prejudice process and parties have nothing to lose if the mediation “fails” and everything to gain if it is successful.

Parliament has since 1994 passed 44 pieces of legislation calling for mediation and moves are afoot to train State Attorneys in mediation.

For Daniel, the ongoing litigation may not bring him any closer to realise his dream to develop the Nkomazi Reserve into a source for national pride and economic opportunities for all in Mpumalanga. For the government, ongoing litigation may harm its reputation and deter potential investors from investing in Mpumulanga.

To ensure that all the relevant parties attend the mediation, Joubert proposed that judge Cornelis Claassen, a retired judge and a trained and accredited mediator, be appointed to arrange a preliminary mediation meeting with the State Attorney and Daniel’s attorney.

Judge Claassen headed the Commission of Inquiry into Ria Phiyega’s conduct, offered to chair the preliminary mediation meeting without charging for his time.

Eventually Daniel & the Mpumalana Tourism authority sat down to a week-long mediation on 22 January and they have reached a settlement by which his frustration will hopefully now be at an end.

But the Protection order against Mabuza must proceed -- Danie's legal strategy seems to coincide with new officials' commitment to rid the province of suspicion.


WHY THE PROTECTION FROM HARASSMENT ACT IS SPECIAL:

Before the Protection from Harassment Act, protection orders were only available to people experiencing physical, sexual, emotional, verbal, psychological, economic and other forms of abuse from a person with whom they had a domestic relationship.

This meant that one could only get a protection order against someone they were married or engaged to; in a romantic, intimate or sexual relationship with; their parent, child or family member, or someone they were living with.

A person wishing to obtain a protection order under this new act does not have to prove the existence of a domestic relationship, which was often a hurdle to obtaining protection in certain situations, such as instances of abuse between an educator and a learner or employer/employee in a whistleblower scenario.

The Protection from Harassment Act allows for a special process where an initial court order is made without the immediate knowledge of the person who is harassing the complainant, based only on the complainant’s side of the story, as long as the court is satisfied that there is prima facie evidence that the complainant is being or may be harassed and that harm is or may be suffered if the protection order isn’t granted immediately.

A future date is then arranged for the person against whom the protection order is sought to oppose the interim protection order being made a final court order.

The court has the powers to prohibit a person from engaging in or attempting to engage in harassment or enlisting the help of another person to engage in harassment or committing in any act specified in the protection order, which means that a protection order can be tailored to the needs of the complainant in his/her specific situation.

At the same time that the protection order is granted, a warrant of arrest may be issued. If the person contravenes the protection order by continuing to harass the complainant, the police may immediately arrest that person.

Failure to comply with the final protection order is a criminal offence and the person may be liable on conduction to a fine or imprisonment for a period not exceeding 5 years.

Press Release:


Protection From Harassment Act
Citing years of harassment, Mpumalanga game reserve owner, Fred Daniel has managed to get an interim protection order against now deputy president David Mabuza who was the former premier of Mpumalanga. After 20 years of struggling through the courts and spending R18-million in legal fees, Daniel has finally broken through against what he calls, ongoing harassment and high-level corruption. But what’s really behind their legal spat?


Script:


SCRIPT: MABUZA PROTECTION ORDER
PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg
PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli
TX: 18 March 2018
DURATION: 11 minutes

VO: Fred Daniel had a big dream. Having made his fortune in information technology, Daniel dreamed of creating a luxurious cross-border game reserve.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: I needed very specific land because I wanted a project that’s interesting. I wanted people to come here and see mountains and rivers and valleys and grasslands.

VO: Daniel found what he was looking for near Badplaas in Mpumalanga. From the late 1990s he bought up farms where agriculture had failed, cleaned up the land and lined up investors. The Development Bank of Southern Africa pledged R135-million. Hotel king Sol Kerzner and Dubai World, R330-million. Cradle of Life was born.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: Sol Kerzner was prepared to build a One And Only on my project. He wanted to build, what he called a Big Five Game Reserve. But he could never build The One and Only because we needed the Big Five permits.

VO: Things started going wrong when Daniel was denied the Big Five permits that would turn a game sanctuary into a world-class attraction. He got bad inspection reports from the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency -- they confiscated some of his animals.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: These civil servants started every trick in the book and they would say there’s a large ban on predators. And then when you go through the process of dealing with that, the next thing they’ll say, oh, there’s a land claim on your property.

VO: Daniel believes he became a target when he blew the whistle that led to investigations into an alleged land claims racket where farm prices were supposedly artificially inflated to line the pockets of a few farmers, businessmen and politicians.
Forensic investigations suggested Mpumalanga premier David Mabuza had become involved. Last week the EFF said a fraud charge it had laid against Mabuza in 2015 is now being considered by prosecutors.

MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Can it be that political bullying has allowed a province as beautiful as Mpumalanga to rot...forcing some politicians to either join in the corruption or neglect service delivery?

VO: Daniel believes Deputy President David Mabuza, then Agriculture MEC, influenced officials to block him. Daniel believes this because some officials told him that they had orders “right from the top” and feared for their jobs and safety.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: Imagine if you’re a civil servant, but you get an instruction from a politician that you will lose your job if you issue Fred Daniel a permit. What are you going to do? You’re going to start looking for excuses, you’re going to start victimising the guy, you’re going to start defaming him and that’s what happened to me.

VO: The land claim on Daniel’s property was shown to be invalid. Over two decades, Daniel spent nearly R20-million battling administrative blockages in court. Desperate, he turned to the 2011 Protection from Harassment Act, often used in cases of domestic violence.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: I realised that the Harassment Act is… is broad...they use words like ‘harm is defined as mental, psychological, physical and economic harm’. And all of those things we’ve suffered.

VO: At the Carolina Magistrates’ Court, Daniel last year obtained interim protection orders against the entire executive of the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency. Boy Nobunga had just been appointed as new CEO.

BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: When I received the Protection Order I was hardly a month if I’m not mistaken, and I had not seen the man and boom, you are then a person who is harassing that person you have never met.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: Some of the things that are stipulated in that is an issue of institutional harassment...does he have merit?

BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: There are issues of characters within the whole story -- it used to be some boys club of people that were working together.

VO: In January, Daniel also asked the court for a protection order against then Premier David Mabuza. Appointed ANC Deputy President in December, Daniel feared Mabuza had the means to make good on alleged threats to drive him out of Badplaas.
Daniel took about 700 pages of forensic reports and affidavits outlining his experiences to court and was granted an interim protection order and suspended warrant of arrest against Mabuza. Jacques Joubert is Daniel’s lawyer.

JACQUES JOUBERT, ATTORNEY: I think Fred is still around because of the Protection Order. I think he was up against and is up against forces that are much more powerful than he is.

VO: A teacher by training, Mabuza rose through the ranks to be appointed Education MEC by Premier Mathews Phosa in 1994. He became Premier in 2009. Daniel’s concerns about his safety and business grew in an atmosphere of fear created by media speculation about corruption and the assassination of whistleblowers and political opponents in inter-ANC conflict in Mpumalanga. Mabuza has always denied any involvement and says such allegations are a smear campaign against him.
Mabuza declined coming on camera on the advice of his legal team. Daniel believes Mabuza instigated land claimants to march on his property. His land was set alight repeatedly; business associates were threatened.

JACQUES JOUBERT: About ten years ago, there was a riot in front of the gate here at Cradle of Life. Mr Mabuza arrived on the scene with a loudhailer and told the people they can stop now, he will make sure they get their land back.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: They cut my fences in broad daylight. They threatened my life. I got a phone call from the local ANC they said Fred, you’re going to get killed. Mabuza told me if I do not admit to this land claim, he cannot protect me (inaudible) community.

JACQUES JOUBERT: He has telephone records of a very heated conversation that he had with Mabuza on the day.

VO: Daniel’s court papers show two phone calls between him and Mabuza that further fuelled Daniel’s fears that there was a conspiracy to drive him out of the area.

JACQUES JOUBERT, ATTORNEY: He’s prepared to take on whoever needs to be taken on, to stand by his rights. I think that he does fear for his life, actually. They’re very aware that they’re living in a province where life can be very cheap.

VO: The Interim Protection Order forbids Mabuza to communicate with Daniel or “insult, intimidate or abuse him in any way”. Last month Mabuza became deputy president of the country. In the run-up to the ANC election, Mabuza’s former boss Mathews Phosa accused him of using a private militia -- like the men firing into the air in this video -- to enforce support from ANC branches. The two men have a history and Mabuza last year unsuccessfully sued Phosa for defamation.

MATHEWS PHOSA: The ANC members in Mpumalanga who don’t like what they see on videos, sent the videos to me and said: Look what’s happening in this province. And we know those people there on the videos, you know, it’s not like we’re guessing -- they are close to David Mabuza! No one has really denied what I said.

VO: Two years ago, Fred Daniel approached Phosa for advice.

MATHEWS PHOSA: He came to me with a whole bucket of problems around the area -- allegations of pieces of land being overvalued and our government being asked to pay inflated prices...I don’t want my government to pay for land more than what it is worth.

VO: He feels claims of corruption and political murders in Mpumalanga must be investigated.

MATHEWS PHOSA: Close to 17 people have died. It’s not allegations. We had to bury those people and they’re all our comrades, we know them. No one has been prosecuted. No inquest has been held. There have been allegations of corruption. All I want is the law enforcement officers to investigate the allegations.

VO: Phosa, a businessman, eventually bought shares in Cradle of Life, the dream that Daniel is still fighting for in court.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: The only protection I had was the judiciary and the only law in South Africa that could protect me so fast was this Harassment Act.

VO: The magistrate ordered Daniel and Mabuza to come to court in February to argue whether the protection order should be made permanent or not. Mabuza’s senior advocate “Denied any threat of harassment”; said Daniel “failed to prove Mabuza’s direct or indirect involvement”; his application was “premised on unsubstantiated speculation and inadmissible evidence” and was an “abuse of the Act and the court process”. He said “the court hadn’t applied its mind” and the interim protection order should be set aside.

MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Is Daniel's use of this law a GENIUS move...cheeky...or is he grasping at straws?

VO: At the Open Democracy Advice Center or ODAC Alison Tilley says citizen whistleblowers have little legal protection -- unlike employees that fall under the Protected Disclosures Act.

ALISON TILLEY, OPEN DEMOCRACY ADVICE CENTRE: ODAC has argued over a number of years that this is a significant gap in the legislation. We certainly have a number instances where whistleblowers have been assassinated. So we are very concerned about their protection. This use of the harassment legislation is novel and we’re not aware of it being used in the ways previously. It certainly would put an interesting remedy in the hands of whistle-blowers.

VO: Joubert urged the court to consider what this decision would mean for whistleblowers in future and said Daniel would only feel safe if his story was public. The matter is postponed until April. Until then, the interim protection order against the Deputy President stands. In a press release, Mabuza said Daniel “made frivolous allegations including defaming me and has committed perjury”.

FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: That affidavit that I did, if there’s one false statement in the affidavit, I can be arrested and go to jail for five years. Now why would I do the trouble to set up a… a very detailed affidavit like that…I don’t want to tarnish anybody’s reputation. I just want to protect my life, my family and my staff.

MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Tourism is the cornerstone of Mpumalanga’s economy but it takes a good relationship between the private sector and government to make it work...but can this partnership survive the fraught relationships of the past?

VO: Last month, Daniel dropped the protection orders against officials because he now has permits, and a restored working relationship.

MACFARLANE MOLELI: As the CEO coming into a mess, what did you have to go into to try and resolve this impasse between the MTPA and Fred Daniels?

BOY NOBUNGA: We got hold of external people to go and do the investigations. He complied, we gave him the licenses.

VO: Nobunga would not comment on the interim order against Mabuza.

BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: The courts are better placed to deal with the matter. If there’s anything that implicates any of the officials in the entity, I would act against those officials. With the interaction that I had with Fred Daniels, he strike me like a person who has passion for the environment and the ideas that he has when implemented, I think they would benefit the province of Mpumalanga and South Africa in general.


PROMOS

10 secs
VO: Deputy President David Mabuza has an interim protection order and suspended warrant of arrest over his head. Is it a political smear campaign, or one man’s legitimate bid for safety?


15 secs
FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: They cut my fences in broad daylight. They threatened my life.
VO: After years of fruitless court action, Mpumalanga businessman Fred Daniel turns to a potentially novel remedy - can the Protection from Harassment Act help him realise his dreams?


15 secs
VO: Why has a Mpumalanga businessman asked the court for a protection order against former Premier David Mabuza, now the Deputy President?
FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: if there’s one false statement in the affidavit, I can go to jail for five years...I don’t want to tarnish anybody’s reputation. I just want to protect my life.

Daniel has been going out of his way to stay out of the courts -- and his efforts finally paid off when he found Stellenbosch attorney Jacques Joubert last year, who specialises in mediation and has been knocking on every door in Mpumalanga to STOP running to court and opposing every action, and sitting down to mediate a way forward. Joubert convinced the new Tourism Management last year that mediation is a private, confidential and without prejudice process and parties have nothing to lose if the mediation “fails” and everything to gain if it is successful. Parliament has since 1994 passed 44 pieces of legislation calling for mediation and moves are afoot to train State Attorneys in mediation. For Daniel, the ongoing litigation may not bring him any closer to realise his dream to develop the Nkomazi Reserve into a source for national pride and economic opportunities for all in Mpumalanga. For the government, ongoing litigation may harm its reputation and deter potential investors from investing in Mpumulanga. To ensure that all the relevant parties attend the mediation, Joubert proposed that judge Cornelis Claassen, a retired judge and a trained and accredited mediator, be appointed to arrange a preliminary mediation meeting with the State Attorney and Daniel’s attorney. Judge Claassen headed the Commission of Inquiry into Ria Phiyega’s conduct, offered to chair the preliminary mediation meeting without charging for his time. Eventually Daniel & the Mpumalana Tourism authority sat down to a week-long mediation on 22 January and they have reached a settlement by which his frustration will hopefully now be at an end. But the Protection order against Mabuza must proceed -- Danie's legal strategy seems to coincide with new officials' commitment to rid the province of suspicion. WHY THE PROTECTION FROM HARASSMENT ACT IS SPECIAL: Before the Protection from Harassment Act, protection orders were only available to people experiencing physical, sexual, emotional, verbal, psychological, economic and other forms of abuse from a person with whom they had a domestic relationship. This meant that one could only get a protection order against someone they were married or engaged to; in a romantic, intimate or sexual relationship with; their parent, child or family member, or someone they were living with. A person wishing to obtain a protection order under this new act does not have to prove the existence of a domestic relationship, which was often a hurdle to obtaining protection in certain situations, such as instances of abuse between an educator and a learner or employer/employee in a whistleblower scenario. The Protection from Harassment Act allows for a special process where an initial court order is made without the immediate knowledge of the person who is harassing the complainant, based only on the complainant’s side of the story, as long as the court is satisfied that there is prima facie evidence that the complainant is being or may be harassed and that harm is or may be suffered if the protection order isn’t granted immediately. A future date is then arranged for the person against whom the protection order is sought to oppose the interim protection order being made a final court order. The court has the powers to prohibit a person from engaging in or attempting to engage in harassment or enlisting the help of another person to engage in harassment or committing in any act specified in the protection order, which means that a protection order can be tailored to the needs of the complainant in his/her specific situation. At the same time that the protection order is granted, a warrant of arrest may be issued. If the person contravenes the protection order by continuing to harass the complainant, the police may immediately arrest that person. Failure to comply with the final protection order is a criminal offence and the person may be liable on conduction to a fine or imprisonment for a period not exceeding 5 years. from Insert in Show: Title Author Last Updated 15 April 2018 - Carte Blanche HD Chwayitisa Futshane 04 May 2018 Press Release: Protection From Harassment Act Citing years of harassment, Mpumalanga game reserve owner, Fred Daniel has managed to get an interim protection order against now deputy president David Mabuza who was the former premier of Mpumalanga. After 20 years of struggling through the courts and spending R18-million in legal fees, Daniel has finally broken through against what he calls, ongoing harassment and high-level corruption. But what’s really behind their legal spat? Script: SCRIPT: MABUZA PROTECTION ORDER PRODUCERS: Anna-Maria van Niekerk & Marzanne van den Berg PRESENTER: Macfarlane Moleli TX: 18 March 2018 DURATION: 11 minutes VO: Fred Daniel had a big dream. Having made his fortune in information technology, Daniel dreamed of creating a luxurious cross-border game reserve. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: I needed very specific land because I wanted a project that’s interesting. I wanted people to come here and see mountains and rivers and valleys and grasslands. VO: Daniel found what he was looking for near Badplaas in Mpumalanga. From the late 1990s he bought up farms where agriculture had failed, cleaned up the land and lined up investors. The Development Bank of Southern Africa pledged R135-million. Hotel king Sol Kerzner and Dubai World, R330-million. Cradle of Life was born. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: Sol Kerzner was prepared to build a One And Only on my project. He wanted to build, what he called a Big Five Game Reserve. But he could never build The One and Only because we needed the Big Five permits. VO: Things started going wrong when Daniel was denied the Big Five permits that would turn a game sanctuary into a world-class attraction. He got bad inspection reports from the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency -- they confiscated some of his animals. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: These civil servants started every trick in the book and they would say there’s a large ban on predators. And then when you go through the process of dealing with that, the next thing they’ll say, oh, there’s a land claim on your property. VO: Daniel believes he became a target when he blew the whistle that led to investigations into an alleged land claims racket where farm prices were supposedly artificially inflated to line the pockets of a few farmers, businessmen and politicians. Forensic investigations suggested Mpumalanga premier David Mabuza had become involved. Last week the EFF said a fraud charge it had laid against Mabuza in 2015 is now being considered by prosecutors. MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Can it be that political bullying has allowed a province as beautiful as Mpumalanga to rot...forcing some politicians to either join in the corruption or neglect service delivery? VO: Daniel believes Deputy President David Mabuza, then Agriculture MEC, influenced officials to block him. Daniel believes this because some officials told him that they had orders “right from the top” and feared for their jobs and safety. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: Imagine if you’re a civil servant, but you get an instruction from a politician that you will lose your job if you issue Fred Daniel a permit. What are you going to do? You’re going to start looking for excuses, you’re going to start victimising the guy, you’re going to start defaming him and that’s what happened to me. VO: The land claim on Daniel’s property was shown to be invalid. Over two decades, Daniel spent nearly R20-million battling administrative blockages in court. Desperate, he turned to the 2011 Protection from Harassment Act, often used in cases of domestic violence. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: I realised that the Harassment Act is… is broad...they use words like ‘harm is defined as mental, psychological, physical and economic harm’. And all of those things we’ve suffered. VO: At the Carolina Magistrates’ Court, Daniel last year obtained interim protection orders against the entire executive of the Mpumalanga Tourism and Parks Agency. Boy Nobunga had just been appointed as new CEO. BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: When I received the Protection Order I was hardly a month if I’m not mistaken, and I had not seen the man and boom, you are then a person who is harassing that person you have never met. MACFARLANE MOLELI: Some of the things that are stipulated in that is an issue of institutional harassment...does he have merit? BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: There are issues of characters within the whole story -- it used to be some boys club of people that were working together. VO: In January, Daniel also asked the court for a protection order against then Premier David Mabuza. Appointed ANC Deputy President in December, Daniel feared Mabuza had the means to make good on alleged threats to drive him out of Badplaas. Daniel took about 700 pages of forensic reports and affidavits outlining his experiences to court and was granted an interim protection order and suspended warrant of arrest against Mabuza. Jacques Joubert is Daniel’s lawyer. JACQUES JOUBERT, ATTORNEY: I think Fred is still around because of the Protection Order. I think he was up against and is up against forces that are much more powerful than he is. VO: A teacher by training, Mabuza rose through the ranks to be appointed Education MEC by Premier Mathews Phosa in 1994. He became Premier in 2009. Daniel’s concerns about his safety and business grew in an atmosphere of fear created by media speculation about corruption and the assassination of whistleblowers and political opponents in inter-ANC conflict in Mpumalanga. Mabuza has always denied any involvement and says such allegations are a smear campaign against him. Mabuza declined coming on camera on the advice of his legal team. Daniel believes Mabuza instigated land claimants to march on his property. His land was set alight repeatedly; business associates were threatened. JACQUES JOUBERT: About ten years ago, there was a riot in front of the gate here at Cradle of Life. Mr Mabuza arrived on the scene with a loudhailer and told the people they can stop now, he will make sure they get their land back. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: They cut my fences in broad daylight. They threatened my life. I got a phone call from the local ANC they said Fred, you’re going to get killed. Mabuza told me if I do not admit to this land claim, he cannot protect me (inaudible) community. JACQUES JOUBERT: He has telephone records of a very heated conversation that he had with Mabuza on the day. VO: Daniel’s court papers show two phone calls between him and Mabuza that further fuelled Daniel’s fears that there was a conspiracy to drive him out of the area. JACQUES JOUBERT, ATTORNEY: He’s prepared to take on whoever needs to be taken on, to stand by his rights. I think that he does fear for his life, actually. They’re very aware that they’re living in a province where life can be very cheap. VO: The Interim Protection Order forbids Mabuza to communicate with Daniel or “insult, intimidate or abuse him in any way”. Last month Mabuza became deputy president of the country. In the run-up to the ANC election, Mabuza’s former boss Mathews Phosa accused him of using a private militia -- like the men firing into the air in this video -- to enforce support from ANC branches. The two men have a history and Mabuza last year unsuccessfully sued Phosa for defamation. MATHEWS PHOSA: The ANC members in Mpumalanga who don’t like what they see on videos, sent the videos to me and said: Look what’s happening in this province. And we know those people there on the videos, you know, it’s not like we’re guessing -- they are close to David Mabuza! No one has really denied what I said. VO: Two years ago, Fred Daniel approached Phosa for advice. MATHEWS PHOSA: He came to me with a whole bucket of problems around the area -- allegations of pieces of land being overvalued and our government being asked to pay inflated prices...I don’t want my government to pay for land more than what it is worth. VO: He feels claims of corruption and political murders in Mpumalanga must be investigated. MATHEWS PHOSA: Close to 17 people have died. It’s not allegations. We had to bury those people and they’re all our comrades, we know them. No one has been prosecuted. No inquest has been held. There have been allegations of corruption. All I want is the law enforcement officers to investigate the allegations. VO: Phosa, a businessman, eventually bought shares in Cradle of Life, the dream that Daniel is still fighting for in court. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: The only protection I had was the judiciary and the only law in South Africa that could protect me so fast was this Harassment Act. VO: The magistrate ordered Daniel and Mabuza to come to court in February to argue whether the protection order should be made permanent or not. Mabuza’s senior advocate “Denied any threat of harassment”; said Daniel “failed to prove Mabuza’s direct or indirect involvement”; his application was “premised on unsubstantiated speculation and inadmissible evidence” and was an “abuse of the Act and the court process”. He said “the court hadn’t applied its mind” and the interim protection order should be set aside. MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Is Daniel's use of this law a GENIUS move...cheeky...or is he grasping at straws? VO: At the Open Democracy Advice Center or ODAC Alison Tilley says citizen whistleblowers have little legal protection -- unlike employees that fall under the Protected Disclosures Act. ALISON TILLEY, OPEN DEMOCRACY ADVICE CENTRE: ODAC has argued over a number of years that this is a significant gap in the legislation. We certainly have a number instances where whistleblowers have been assassinated. So we are very concerned about their protection. This use of the harassment legislation is novel and we’re not aware of it being used in the ways previously. It certainly would put an interesting remedy in the hands of whistle-blowers. VO: Joubert urged the court to consider what this decision would mean for whistleblowers in future and said Daniel would only feel safe if his story was public. The matter is postponed until April. Until then, the interim protection order against the Deputy President stands. In a press release, Mabuza said Daniel “made frivolous allegations including defaming me and has committed perjury”. FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: That affidavit that I did, if there’s one false statement in the affidavit, I can be arrested and go to jail for five years. Now why would I do the trouble to set up a… a very detailed affidavit like that…I don’t want to tarnish anybody’s reputation. I just want to protect my life, my family and my staff. MACFARLANE MOLELI LINK TO CAMERA: Tourism is the cornerstone of Mpumalanga’s economy but it takes a good relationship between the private sector and government to make it work...but can this partnership survive the fraught relationships of the past? VO: Last month, Daniel dropped the protection orders against officials because he now has permits, and a restored working relationship. MACFARLANE MOLELI: As the CEO coming into a mess, what did you have to go into to try and resolve this impasse between the MTPA and Fred Daniels? BOY NOBUNGA: We got hold of external people to go and do the investigations. He complied, we gave him the licenses. VO: Nobunga would not comment on the interim order against Mabuza. BOY NOBUNGA, CEO, MPUMALANGA TOURISM AND PARKS AGENCY: The courts are better placed to deal with the matter. If there’s anything that implicates any of the officials in the entity, I would act against those officials. With the interaction that I had with Fred Daniels, he strike me like a person who has passion for the environment and the ideas that he has when implemented, I think they would benefit the province of Mpumalanga and South Africa in general. PROMOS 10 secs VO: Deputy President David Mabuza has an interim protection order and suspended warrant of arrest over his head. Is it a political smear campaign, or one man’s legitimate bid for safety? 15 secs FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: They cut my fences in broad daylight. They threatened my life. VO: After years of fruitless court action, Mpumalanga businessman Fred Daniel turns to a potentially novel remedy - can the Protection from Harassment Act help him realise his dreams? 15 secs VO: Why has a Mpumalanga businessman asked the court for a protection order against former Premier David Mabuza, now the Deputy President? FRED DANIEL, OWNER, CRADLE OF LIFE: if there’s one false statement in the affidavit, I can go to jail for five years...I don’t want to tarnish anybody’s reputation. I just want to protect my life.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Has one man's long lonely battle to build his dream Big-5 reserve inadvertently opened a way for ordinary people to hit back decisively against corruption?
metadata.Unique Selling Point: After 20 years of struggling through the courts, spending R18-million in legal fees to defend his actions to establish a luxury Big-5 game Nkomazi Game reserve, Cradle of Life, Mpumalanga businessman Fred Daniel has finally broken through against ongoing harassment and high-level corruption that have nearly scuppered his life’s work – by applying a simple, inexpensive and bold law. Conservationist Fred Daniel made his fortune in IT and dreamed of establishing a big-5 game reserve near Badplaas, Mpumalanga. He had all the partnerships and international deals in place to make it happen. Daniel bought up 98 failing farms near Badplaas – it had become impossible to cultivate grain here, and farmers were eager to sell up and get out. But since Day One, Daniel has found himself at the receiving end of administrative blockages, violence, victimisation and harassment, last year there was an attempted media smear campaign with false allegations that Daniel had to refute by opening his gates and books to the media. And he's even had a phone call from one David Mabuza, then MEC for Agriculture, to get out of Badplaas. He couldn’t get his Big-5 permits. He had his boundary fences cut. There were attempts to burn down his buildings. He woke up to violent protests on his doorstep. He had his animals removed and sold off with the money diverted to the Problem Animal Fund. And then there was the fraudulent land claim against his land -- the scandal that saw the department of rural development and land reform buying farms for claimant communities at rates that were up to 300% higher than market value. Daniel hired forensic investigators and exposed the fraudulent land claim (in 2003), with tentacles reaching into the then MEC for Agriculture, DD Mabuza’s office. If Daniel hadn't exposed it, the tax payer would have lost R600million. Since then Parliament have even passed the Restitution of Land Rights Amendment Act, 2014 which provides that anyone who lodges a claim with the intention of defrauding the state shall be guilty of an offence and liable on conviction to a fine and imprisonment. (Two years ago the Land Claims Court in Randburg ordered Rural Development and Land Reform Minister Gugile Nkwinti to take back the land that was given to a controversial trust and review the claim. The validity of the claim involving 105 farms worth R51 million in Mpumalanga’s Badplaas area had been contested over the past 12 years.) But none such provisions protected Daniel when he turned whistleblower. Daniel's whistleblowing, together with defrauded land claimants, resulted the scheme exposed and a R3.3 million fraud charge being laid by the EFF against Mpumalanga Premier David Mabuza (http://city-press.news24.com/News/r33m-haunts-premier-mabuza-20151212). But by then, Daniel's investors, and potential partners had vanished. But all hell broke loose. Harassment escalated sharply. Of 20 court cases where Daniel opposed the Mpumalanga tourism authorities’ administrative interference, he won 18. In the process he spent over R18-million. In forensic reports and court proceedings, all of which Daniel paid for, testimony emanated that officials had suffered immense political pressure, all the way to the Premier's office, to thwart Cradle of Life. Now, only two cases remain outstanding: - a R1,6bn damages claim against the government for the business he’s lost (mediation process is underway to try and settle this and restore relationships with new Tourism Authority management who are eager to help him). - an interim protection order against the same DD Mabuza – now Premier of Mpumalanga and Deputy President of the ANC.
metadata.Summary: This is a story of Fred Daniel’s breakthrough after 20 years of legal struggles – through the clever, lateral application of the relatively simple Protection from Harassment Act (17 of 2011) which came into effect in 2013 to stop and fix harassment and stalking behaviour which violate someone’s Constitutional right to privacy and dignity. After spending millions on legal representatives, investigations and getting nowhere, this Act provided for Daniel an inexpensive civil remedy to protect him from behaviour which may not constitute a crime but may impact negatively on various rights... All he had to do was fill out a simple form, available online, and put his case to a Magistrate – which Daniel did in Carolina. He didn’t even need legal representation. And his harasser didn't have to be present. The only risk...if Daniel is lying, he could himself face arrest. On Monday 29 January, the Carolina Magistrate granted Daniel his interim protection order, and the court has invited Mr Mabuza to court on 19 Feb to explain why the order shouldn’t be made permanent.
